stories.headline: OIL TUMBLES ON REPORTS OF PAKISTAN-BROKERED IRAN TALKS AS TRUMP WEIGHS DEEPER STRIKES
stories.body: Brent crude fell nearly 4% to settle at $96.78 a barrel and WTI dropped 3.0% to $89.31 after Reuters reported Pakistan, backed by China, is exploring a path to restart stalled US-Iran talks - even as the New York Times reported Trump met his national security team Friday to weigh escalating US strikes on Iran for a 13th straight day. It was Brent's biggest one-day drop since late June.
stories.explain: The reversal shows how much of oil's run toward $100 this week was a war-risk premium rather than an actual supply loss - the moment traders saw a credible off-ramp, that premium unwound almost as fast as it built, even though not a single barrel of physical flow has changed yet. Futures and options price geopolitical risk asymmetrically: bad news gets priced in immediately on fear of worse to come, while de-escalation headlines get discounted more slowly until confirmed, which is why today's drop only unwound about a third of the week's gain. For a market watching next week's FOMC, cheaper oil is a genuine relief valve - it strips out the freshest inflationary impulse the Fed would otherwise have had to weigh six days before its decision.

stories.headline: FED HIKE ODDS FOR NEXT WEEK'S MEETING JUMP TO ROUGHLY 1-IN-3 AS INFLATION HAWKS GAIN GROUND
stories.body: Markets are now pricing roughly a one-in-three chance the Fed raises rates at its July 28-29 meeting under Chair Kevin Warsh, up from near 18% earlier this month, after Governor Lisa Cook flagged inflation running at 3.7% - nearly double the Fed's 2% target - and Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and Governor Christopher Waller both warned policy may need reconsidering if price pressures don't cool.
stories.explain: A hike is still the minority outcome, but the size of the swing - odds roughly doubling in three weeks - shows the committee's internal debate shifting from 'how many cuts' to 'do we even hold,' a meaningfully more hawkish reaction function than markets had priced entering July. Fed funds futures translate directly into a hike probability because each contract settles on the realized average rate for that month, so a jump in the implied yield on the July contract mechanically shows up as higher hike odds. Today's oil-driven relief in headline prices cuts the other way heading into the meeting, handing doves fresh ammunition just as the hawkish case looked to be building momentum.

stories.headline: CHIP STOCKS SINK NASDAQ 100 1.1% EVEN AS DOW REBOUNDS ON APPLE'S 3.5% RALLY
stories.body: The Nasdaq 100 fell about 1.1% to roughly 28,060 as Intel dropped 7.9% despite issuing a blockbuster revenue forecast and Sandisk tumbled nearly 11% alongside other memory names, while the Dow gained 0.46% to 51,947 and the S&P 500 finished essentially flat (+0.05% to 7,412) as Apple's 3.5% jump offset the semiconductor rout.
stories.explain: Intel selling off on a beat-and-raise is a valuation story, not an earnings story: when a stock trades at a premium built on AI-driven demand assumptions, guidance that's merely 'great' instead of 'extraordinary' can still disappoint expectations already baked into the price. The divergence between chips and blue chips also reflects rotation - money moving out of the most AI-capex-exposed names and into steadier cash-generative names like Apple - exactly the kind of sector dispersion that shows up when a market's leadership narrative starts to wobble without the index itself breaking down. Watch whether that rotation persists into next week's FOMC; a market nervous about both rate risk and AI-spending discipline at once tends to punish richly valued growth names hardest.

stories.headline: BOFA BULL & BEAR INDICATOR HITS ITS MOST BULLISH READING SINCE 2021, FLASHING A CONTRARIAN SELL SIGNAL
stories.body: Bank of America's closely watched Bull & Bear Indicator climbed to its highest level since 2021 this week, a threshold that has historically preceded market pullbacks, as investors pile into risk assets even while flagging concern over the scale of AI-related capital spending across megacap tech.
stories.explain: The indicator is a contrarian tool by design - it aggregates positioning, flows, and breadth, and BofA's own research triggers a 'sell' signal once extreme bullishness is reached, on the theory that when everyone who wants to be long already is, there's limited new buying power left to push prices higher. Its last comparable reading in 2021 preceded a significant multi-month correction, though the indicator has also given false signals during strong bull markets, so it's a warning about positioning fragility rather than a timing call. Paired with today's AI-capex anxiety and chip-sector weakness, it suggests the market's cushion against a negative surprise - on rates, on earnings, or on oil - is thinner than it's been in years.

stories.headline: 5-STAR 2027 PG CAYDEN DAUGHTRY IGNITES BLUE-BLOOD BIDDING WAR AFTER RECORD-SHATTERING PEACH JAM
stories.body: Daughtry led the Florida Rebels to the Nike EYBL Peach Jam championship while averaging 32.3 points, 6.1 assists, 4.9 rebounds and 2.9 steals over his final eight games on 59% shooting, rocketing him to No. 3 in the 2027 class and setting off an active recruiting battle led by Kentucky, which extended an offer in May.

stories.headline: LEBRON JAMES SIGNS WITH 76ERS FOR HISTORIC 24TH SEASON, CALLS IT HIS 'LAST DECISION'
stories.body: James agreed to a two-year, $8 million deal with Philadelphia after telling the Lakers he wouldn't return, ending an eight-year run in LA that included the 2020 title; the 41-year-old four-time champion said he believes he can help make the 76ers 'a championship team' as he begins an unprecedented 24th NBA season.

stories.headline: PANTHERS' NIC SCOURTON TEARS ACL ON DAY ONE OF TRAINING CAMP AS ALL 32 TEAMS OPEN CAMP
stories.body: Carolina's second-year edge rusher, who posted 47 tackles and five sacks as a 2025 rookie starter, tore his ACL on a wet field during Thursday's opening practice - a major blow opposite newly signed Jaelan Phillips - as all 32 NFL teams report to camp by July 28, with Chiefs QB Patrick Mahomes separately confirming he's been cleared to practice after his December ACL/LCL tear.

stories.headline: SEC MEDIA DAYS WRAP IN TAMPA WITH LANE KIFFIN'S LSU DEBUT AND A THREE-YEAR TITLE DROUGHT LOOMING
stories.body: The four-day SEC Media Days closed Thursday in Tampa with LSU, Arkansas, Mississippi State and Texas taking the podium, headlined by Lane Kiffin's first appearance as LSU's coach after his move from Ole Miss; the conference enters its first nine-game schedule with six new head coaches and no national title since the 2022 season, as the Big Ten has won the last three championships.

sports.detail: Landed 4-star CB Censere Gaylord as Jedd Fisch's staff fills out the class. Season opens with the Apple Cup vs. Washington State, moved to Sunday, Sept. 6 at Husky Stadium.
Croatian forward Boris Tišma committed as Danny Sprinkle rebuilds after a 16-17 season. Forward Hannes Steinbach went No. 14 to the Hornets in the 2026 NBA Draft.

Defending Super Bowl LX champs opened camp Friday as veterans reported. Season opens Sept. 9 vs. New England in a Super Bowl rematch; several players and coaches attended Monday's Mariners game with the Lombardi Trophy.

Coming off a 60-win season, Detroit added Isaiah Joe, John Collins, Gary Harris and Taurean Prince (CBS gave the offseason a 'C'). RFA center Jalen Duren remains at a standstill with the team; talks could stretch into August.

Mariners (51-52) dropped the series to Cincinnati on Sal Stewart's go-ahead three-run homer in a 5-3 loss Wednesday, sitting one game back of Texas in the AL West. Bryce Miller (4-4, 2.27 ERA) starts tonight's series opener at Rangers.

Big Ten Media Days begin Tuesday, July 28 in Chicago
Seahawks training camp runs through Aug. 13 ahead of the Sept. 9 opener vs. New England

deepDive.title: How a Geopolitical Risk Premium Gets Priced Into Oil — and Unwound Just as Fast
content: Today's brief captures the whole cycle in one week: Brent flirted with $100 a barrel as Houthi strikes and a Red Sea blockade raised fears of a real supply disruption, then dropped almost 4% today the moment Reuters reported Pakistan, backed by China, was pushing to restart US-Iran talks. Nothing about the physical oil market changed between Thursday and Friday - no tanker was freed, no sanction was lifted - yet the price moved nearly $4 a barrel on a single sourced report. That gap between the size of the price move and the size of the underlying news is the signature of a risk premium doing exactly what it's supposed to do: repricing probability, not physical barrels.

Mechanically, a geopolitical risk premium lives in the front of the futures curve, because that's where supply disruptions would first show up in deliverable barrels. Traders essentially build a probability-weighted estimate: some chance of a Hormuz or Bab el-Mandeb closure that removes millions of barrels a day, multiplied by how severe and how long that closure might last, added on top of the 'fundamental' price justified by current supply and demand. When headlines raise the odds of disruption, the premium expands; when a credible de-escalation path appears, traders cut that probability estimate and the premium contracts - even though, as today showed, it rarely unwinds in full on one headline, since the underlying conflict hasn't actually resolved.

The clearest historical analog is the September 2019 Abqaiq-Khurais attack, which knocked out roughly 5% of global oil supply overnight and sent Brent up nearly 15% in a single session - the largest one-day jump on record at the time. Yet within three weeks, prices had round-tripped back to pre-attack levels once Saudi Arabia restored production faster than feared, even though the attack itself was real and the barrels genuinely went offline. That episode is the cleanest proof that oil's headline-driven moves are about revised expectations of future supply, not a simple tally of barrels lost today - a distinction that matters as much for a threatened blockade as for an actual strike.

For next week's FOMC, this mechanism has direct teeth: energy prices flow into headline CPI within one to two months, and this week's spike toward $100 had already become a talking point for hawks pushing for a July hike. Today's pullback to under $90 doesn't erase that data point, but it does soften the inflation case just six days before the meeting, giving doves something concrete to point to. The lesson for reading any oil headline going forward is the same one this week just demonstrated twice: ask whether the news changes the physical flow of barrels or just the market's estimate of the odds - because the price reaction to the second kind can be just as large, and just as reversible.
